title: A Book That Would Not Burn
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The fire had reached the ledger, but it hadn't finished the job.

That was how Severus described it when Neri carried the old volume into Moonroot Archive. Its cover was black along one edge, the binding split, and half the pages were stuck together by smoke and water. It smelled unpleasantly of damp ash.

"I was hoping you could read it," Neri said.

Severus examined the book without touching the damaged edge.

"You were hoping I could make it tell you what you want to know."

Neri's face tightened.

"Is there a difference?"

"An enormous one."

I laid clean paper on the worktable and moved the kettle away. The archive's west room was cool enough to keep glue from softening and dry enough for careful examination. At least, it was when Pip remembered to close the upper windows.

"What do we know?" I asked.

Neri looked toward the door.

"During the Closed Bells, a decision was made to seal the lower maintenance route. The public record shows the date of the order, but the name of the person who authorized it is missing."

"Missing?" Severus asked.

"Scratched out."

"Then let us call it scratched out."

I wrote the words down.

That mattered. A missing name might have been lost accidentally. A name removed by someone's hand meant somebody had chosen for the record to become incomplete.

We began with photographs. Danse had lent the archive a simple stand to hold the camera steady. Tamsin had built a cradle so the book would not be forced flat. We recorded the cover, the water stains, and the burned margins before opening the first page.

Severus prepared a small solution to test ink on a separate damaged scrap. He did not pour anything onto the ledger.

"You look disappointed," he said.

"I was hoping for a dramatic spell," I admitted.

"A dramatic spell would be an efficient way to destroy irreplaceable evidence."

"That was my second guess."

He looked at me over his spectacles.

"Your guesses are improving."

We spent an hour turning pages with a thin support beneath each one. Most were ordinary maintenance records: stone deliveries, canal cleanings, broken latches, a note about replacing bell ropes after a storm. The mundanity was almost comforting.

Then we reached the page with the blank line.

The date was written in brown ink. The instruction said to close the lower route until the flood had passed. Beneath it, where a name should have been, the paper was rough and pale.

Neri leaned closer.

"That is it."

I studied the mark.

It hadn't been rubbed away completely. A few threads of ink clung near the left margin.

"Can we recover it?" I asked.

"Possibly," Severus said. "But recovery is not the same as interpretation."

He tested the page under angled light, then with a lens. The surface showed signs of scraping. Along one edge, a faint mark remained from the original pressure of the pen.

"It may have been a signature," he said.

"Whose?" Neri asked.

"Not yet an answer."

Neri went quiet.

I felt the weight of their frustration. People had died or been prevented from leaving during the Closed Bells. The valley had told the story as a warning, but too many of the specific decisions had vanished behind phrases like necessary precautions.

It was tempting to put a name in the blank and make the uncertainty end.

Severus closed the lens case.

"We need independent records."

Neri shook their head.

"The official copies burned."

"Then we look for records that were not official."

I thought of Fen's tide charts. The old cart invoices. The private departure register that had once expected people to return, whether they wanted to or not.

"Maintenance bills," I said. "A closure order would have needed materials. Locks, hinges, sealing stone. Somebody paid for them."

Severus turned toward me.

"Excellent."

I tried not to look too pleased.

We spent the afternoon following money.

Mara brought an old bakery account book that mentioned feeding an extra work crew during the flood. Tamsin found a receipt for iron fittings in a private box. Fen produced a copy of a tide measurement showing the lower route had been sealed before the highest water arrived.

None of those records named the person who gave the order.

Together, they changed the story.

The route had not been shut only because the flood had reached its worst point. It had been shut earlier, when officials were frightened of what might happen and had begun restricting movement.

Neri sat down.

"I remember the fear," they said. "I remember people arguing. Some wanted to keep the doors open. Others said the panic would kill us."

"Who was in charge?" I asked.

They looked at me.

"I cannot yet give a reliable answer."

I heard how carefully they had chosen the word reliable.

Severus did too.

"Then do not manufacture one," he said.

The room was quiet.

After a while Neri asked whether the evidence should be displayed at the next council meeting.

"Show what we know," I said. "Not a guessed signature. Include the scratched line. Include the invoices. And invite testimony from people affected by the closure, with their permission."

Severus nodded.

"An honest gap is more useful than a persuasive falsehood."

We prepared a report with clear labels: confirmed, corroborated, unverified. A warning at the top explained that the ledger's damaged condition limited the conclusions anyone could draw.

The work took longer than the committee wanted.

That felt appropriate.

When Neri left, the archive was dark except for one lamp over the table. Severus stood beside the ledger, looking at the scraped line.

"People are fond of histories with a villain named in the first sentence," he said.

"Are you thinking about your own?"

His face changed.

"Among others."

I did not press.

He looked toward the window.

"I have been praised for choices that harmed people. Condemned for actions I did not take. Sometimes both by the same person, depending on which version of the story they preferred."

"Does that make the truth less important?"

"Quite the opposite."

I stepped beside him.

"I'm glad you told Neri to leave the gap."

He looked at me.

"Are you praising my restraint?"

"Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late."

I smiled.

He touched my hand, the lightest pressure of his fingers against mine. Then he took off his spectacles and set them beside the ledger.

"I had been looking forward to an evening with you," he said.

"You have one."

"After this?"

"Especially after this."

He leaned close. His kiss was gentle, touched with the faint warmth of tea and the sharper scent of paper dust. I put my hand against his chest and felt him relax.

"Come home," I said.

He glanced at the old book.

"It will be here tomorrow."

"Yes."

He nodded, as though he were still getting used to the idea that leaving work unfinished did not mean abandoning it.

We covered the ledger, locked the archive, and walked through the Moonroot Door.

In the morning, the book remained exactly where it belonged: damaged, preserved, and still capable of telling a story without pretending it could tell all of one.
